<!-- source: https://docs.cartesi.io/cartesi-rollups/2.0/development/Advanced-configuration/ -->

---
id: Advanced-configuration
title: Advanced configuration
resources:
---

When you build an application with the Cartesi CLI, the CLI needs to know how to set up your Cartesi Machine. Things like how much memory to allocate, what code to run, and what data to include. All of these choices live in a single file at the root of your project called `cartesi.toml`.

If you have worked with configuration files like `docker-compose.yml` or `Cargo.toml`, the idea is the same. You describe what you want, and the CLI takes care of the rest.

The `cartesi.toml` file is written in [TOML](https://toml.io), a minimal and readable configuration format. You do not need to be a TOML expert to use it. If you can read key value pairs, you are good to go.

Here is what the file controls at a high level:

- **SDK version**: Which version of the Cartesi SDK to use when building your machine.
- **Machine settings**: How the machine boots, how much RAM it has, what program it runs, and how it behaves.
- **Drives**: The file systems attached to your machine, including your application code and any additional data.

`cartesi build`, `cartesi shell` and `cartesi run` read `cartesi.toml` (`cartesi run` reads the `sdk` key and the `[withdrawal]` and `[prt]` tables, and rejects invalid keys); other commands, such as `cartesi hash`, `cartesi send` and `cartesi deposit`, read only the `sdk` key. By default, the CLI looks for a `cartesi.toml` in the project root, unless you point it to a different path using the `-c` or `--config` flag with a relative path to the configuration file. If no config file is found, the CLI applies sensible defaults, most of which are covered in the sections below. The default Cartesi templates do not include a `cartesi.toml` in the project root hence you manually create a configuration file when you have an explicit need for it.

## Getting Started with Minimal Configuration

You do not need to fill out every field to get started. In fact, the simplest `cartesi.toml` file can be completely empty, or even absent altogether. The CLI will apply defaults for everything.

Here is what the defaults look like behind the scenes:

```toml
sdk = "cartesi/sdk:<version>"

[machine]
ram_length = "128Mi"
use_docker_env = true
use_docker_workdir = true

[drives.root]
builder = "docker"
dockerfile = "Dockerfile"
format = "ext2"
```

This means that by default, the CLI will:

1. Use the default SDK version of your CLI release (for example, `cartesi/sdk:0.12.0-alpha.45` for Cartesi CLI 2.0.0-alpha.42, which ships rollups-node v2.0.0-alpha.14 and Cartesi Machine emulator 0.22.0).
2. Give your machine 128 megabytes of RAM.
3. Build your root drive from a `Dockerfile` in your project directory.
4. Pull environment variables and the working directory from that Docker image.
5. Enable rollup mode so your app can process inputs from the blockchain.

If those defaults work for you, all you need is a `Dockerfile` and you are ready to build. As your project grows, you can override any of these values by adding them to your `cartesi.toml`.

## SDK Version

```toml
sdk = "cartesi/sdk:<version>"
```

The `sdk` field tells the CLI which version of the Cartesi SDK image to use when building your machine. This is a docker image containing the Linux kernel, the RISC‑V toolchain, Cartesi Node and everything else needed to assemble your Cartesi Machine.

Think of it as pinning a version of your build environment. If you are working on a team, setting this explicitly ensures everyone builds with the same SDK, avoiding the classic "it works on my machine" problem. Each SDK is tied to a Cartesi CLI version, hence it's important you have a compatible CLI installed for the sdk version you specify. When you omit the SDK field the CLI uses its own built in default version.

The SDK image also decides which Cartesi Machine emulator builds your machine, and a node can only load machines built with its own emulator line. These docs target rollups-node v2.0.0-alpha.14 (emulator 0.22.0), which is what the default SDK of Cartesi CLI 2.0.0-alpha.42 builds for. To keep the build reproducible when the CLI is upgraded, pin it:

```toml
sdk = "cartesi/sdk:0.12.0-alpha.45"
```

**When to change this:** When there's a new SDK version and you want to adopt it, or when you need to stay on a specific version for compatibility.

## Machine Configuration

The `[machine]` section controls how your Cartesi Machine is set up and how it behaves at runtime. This is where you configure the virtual computer that runs your application.

```toml
[machine]
```

### Entrypoint

```toml
entrypoint = "rollup-init /usr/local/bin/python3 /opt/cartesi/dapp/dapp.py"
```

The `entrypoint` tells the machine which program to run when it starts up. This is the path to your application binary inside the machine's file system.

If you are building your root drive from a Docker image (which is the default), you may not need to set this at all. The CLI can pick up the entrypoint from your Dockerfile's `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD` instructions. You would set this explicitly when you want to override whatever the Docker image defines, or when your setup does not use Docker.

The `entrypoint` replaces the image's `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD`. An application that talks to the rollup HTTP server (`ROLLUP_HTTP_SERVER_URL`), as the C++, Go, Python and Rust templates do, must be started through `rollup-init`, which starts the server and then runs your program, as the templates' Dockerfiles do with `ENTRYPOINT ["rollup-init"]`. Without it, the server is not running and the build fails when the application calls `/finish`.

### Boot Arguments

```toml
boot_args = ["no4lvl", "quiet", "earlycon=sbi", "console=hvc0", "rootfstype=ext2", "root=/dev/pmem0", "rw", "init=/usr/sbin/cartesi-init"]
```

These are Linux kernel boot arguments passed to the machine when it starts. They control low level behavior like which console to use, what file system type the root drive is, and where to find the init process. The CLI appends them to the default kernel command line of the machine; it does not replace it.

For most applications, you will never need to touch this. The defaults work well for typical setups. This field exists for advanced use cases where you need fine grained control over the kernel's boot process, such as changing the root file system type or adjusting console output behavior.

Each argument is a string in the array. The order does not matter to the kernel, but keeping them organized helps readability.

### Memory Settings

```toml
ram_length = "128Mi"
ram_image = "/usr/share/cartesi-machine/images/linux.bin"
```

**`ram_length`** sets how much RAM your Cartesi Machine has. The default is `128Mi` (128 mebibytes). You can use human readable sizes like `"64Mi"`, `"256Mi"`, or `"1Gi"`.

Exact RAM requirements are unique for each application. A lightweight app that processes small inputs might be fine with 64Mi. A machine learning model or an application that handles large data structures might need 256Mi or more. It's important to stress test your application during development and testing to figure out an optimal RAM configuration for your application.

**`ram_image`** specifies the path to the Linux kernel binary used inside the machine. This path points to a location inside the SDK image, not on your local file system. You almost never need to change this unless you are working with a custom kernel.

### Execution Limits

```toml
max_mcycle = 10000000000
```

The `max_mcycle` field sets the maximum machine cycle of the run that `cartesi build` performs to boot the machine until it waits for its first input (the manual `rx-accepted` yield). Once the machine reaches this limit, it stops, and the build stores the machine in that state. Such a machine cannot process inputs, so combine `max_mcycle` with `assert_rolling_template = true` to make the build fail instead. The limit is not stored in the machine and does not bound the processing of inputs, which the node limits with its own execution parameters.

When `max_mcycle` is omitted, the CLI sets no limit. The value must be an integer of at most `9007199254740991` (2^53 - 1): the CLI rejects larger TOML integers with `integer value cannot be represented losslessly`.

### Rollup Behavior

```toml
assert_rolling_template = true
```

**`assert_rolling_template`** is related to rolling template assertions. When set to `true`, the build fails if the machine is not compatible with Rolling Cartesi Machine templates, that is, if it does not stop at a manual `rx-accepted` yield, the point where a rollups application waits for its first input. Use it to catch, at build time, an application that would not be able to process inputs.

### Docker Integration

```toml
use_docker_env = true
use_docker_workdir = true
user = "dapp"
```

These fields control how the CLI uses information from your Docker image when building the machine.

**`use_docker_env`** (default: `true`) tells the CLI to inject the environment variables defined in your Docker image (via `ENV` instructions) into the Cartesi Machine. This means if your Dockerfile sets `ENV APP_MODE=production`, that variable will be available to your application inside the machine.

**`use_docker_workdir`** (default: `true`) tells the CLI to use the `WORKDIR` from your Docker image as the working directory inside the machine. This keeps your Docker and Cartesi environments consistent.

**`user`** sets the user that your application runs as inside the machine. The default value `"dapp"` is a non root user, which is a good security practice. You can change this if your application needs to run as a different user.

### Final Hash

`cartesi build` always stores the machine together with its final hash. This hash uniquely identifies the exact state of your Cartesi Machine, including all its drives, memory, and configuration.

This is important for on chain verification. The hash is what gets registered on the blockchain as the application's template hash, and it allows anyone to verify that the machine running off chain is exactly the same one that was agreed upon. When you deploy, `cartesi-rollups-cli deploy application` reads the template hash from the stored machine, and by default the node refuses to run a machine whose hash does not match the registered one. This applies to every deployment, whether on a local devnet, a testnet or mainnet.

There is no `final_hash` option to set: it was removed in Cartesi CLI 2.0.0-alpha.16, and since 2.0.0-alpha.41 `cartesi build` fails on unknown keys such as `final_hash`. Remove it from older `cartesi.toml` files.

## Drives

Drives are the file systems attached to your Cartesi Machine. Since the machine is a virtual computer, drives are its hard disks. Every machine has at least one drive (the root drive), and it can have up to 8 drives in total, the root drive included.

Each drive has a name and is defined under `[drives.<name>]`. The name is used as an identifier and, by default, determines where the drive is mounted inside the machine at `/mnt/<name>`.

The key decision for each drive is its **builder**, which tells the CLI how to create the drive image. There are five builder types:

| Builder     | What it does                            |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `docker`    | Builds the drive from a Dockerfile      |
| `empty`     | Creates a blank drive of a given size   |
| `directory` | Packages a local directory into a drive |
| `tar`       | Creates a drive from a tar archive      |
| `none`      | Uses an existing drive image file as is |

Let's walk through each one.

### The Root Drive

```toml
[drives.root]
builder = "docker"
dockerfile = "Dockerfile"
format = "ext2"
extra_size = "100Mb"
```

The root drive is special. It is the main file system of your Cartesi Machine, the one that contains your operating system, libraries, and application code. It is always named `root`, and if you do not define it in your `cartesi.toml`, the CLI creates one automatically using the Docker builder.

### Docker Builder

```toml
[drives.root]
builder = "docker"
dockerfile = "Dockerfile"
target = "docker-multi-stage-target"
format = "ext2"
extra_size = "100Mb"
```

The Docker builder is the most common and the default for the root drive. It builds a drive image from a Dockerfile, which means you can use all the Docker features you already know: multi stage builds, package managers, `COPY` instructions, and so on.

**`dockerfile`** is the path to your Dockerfile, relative to your project root. Defaults to `"Dockerfile"`.

**`target`** lets you specify a build target in a multi stage Dockerfile. If your Dockerfile has multiple stages (`FROM ... AS builder`, `FROM ... AS runtime`), you can tell the CLI which stage to use for the drive. If you leave this out, the CLI uses the last stage.

**`format`** sets the file system format for the drive image. You have two choices:

- `"ext2"` (default): A standard read/write Linux file system. Use this when your application needs to write to the drive at runtime.
- `"sqfs"` (SquashFS): A compressed, read only file system. Use this when your drive contains static data that will not change. It produces smaller images.

**`extra_size`** adds extra free space to the drive beyond what your files actually need. The value is a string like `"100Mb"` or `"50Mi"`. This is useful when your application creates temporary files or writes logs at runtime and needs room to do so.

### Empty Builder

```toml
[drives.data]
builder = "empty"
size = "100Mb"
mount = "/var/lib/app"
```

The empty builder creates a blank drive with no files on it. This is useful when your application needs a writable space to store data at runtime, like a database, cache, or scratch space.

**`size`** is required and sets the total size of the drive. You can specify it as a string like `"100Mb"` or as a number in bytes.

**`mount`** sets where the drive appears inside the machine's file system. If you omit it, the drive is mounted at `/mnt/<name>`, where `<name>` is whatever you called the drive in your configuration. In this example, the drive would be available at `/var/lib/app`.

### Directory Builder

```toml
[drives.data]
builder = "directory"
directory = "./data"
extra_size = "100Mb"
format = "ext2"
mount = "/var/lib/app_two"
```

The directory builder takes a folder from your local machine and packages it into a drive image. This is a straightforward way to include data files, configuration, or any other content without going through Docker.

**`directory`** is required and points to the local folder you want to package. The path is relative to your project root.

**`extra_size`** adds breathing room beyond the actual size of the directory's contents. Optional, defaults to zero. With the `ext2` format, a drive built with no extra space can fail with `xgenext2fs: too few blocks`; set a small `extra_size` in that case.

**`format`** works the same as with the Docker builder: `"ext2"` for read/write, `"sqfs"` for read only compressed.

**`mount`** sets the mount point inside the machine. Optional, defaults to `/mnt/<name>`.

### Tar Builder

```toml
[drives.data]
builder = "tar"
filename = "build/files.tar"
extra_size = "100Mb"
mount = "/var/lib/app_three"
```

The tar builder creates a drive from a tar archive. This is handy when your build process already produces a `.tar` file, or when you want to bundle files from a CI pipeline into a drive without needing Docker or a directory on disk.

**`filename`** is required and points to the `.tar` file, relative to your project root.

**`extra_size`** adds extra space on top of the archive contents.

**`mount`** sets the mount point inside the machine. Optional, defaults to `/mnt/<name>`.

### Pre built Drive (None Builder)

```toml
[drives.doom]
builder = "none"
filename = "./games/doom.sqfs"
mount = "/usr/local/games/doom"
```

The none builder skips building entirely. It takes an existing drive image file and attaches it to the machine as is. This is useful when you have a pre built file system image, perhaps from another tool, a third party, or a previous build. Note that `doom` is a placeholder for a sample directory name, in your case all instances would be replaced with an appropriate name.

**`filename`** is required and points to the existing image file. The file extension determines the format: `.ext2` for ext2 and `.sqfs` for SquashFS.

**`mount`** sets the mount point inside the machine. Optional, defaults to `/mnt/<name>`.

This builder is great for including large, static assets that you do not want to rebuild every time. In the example above, a pre built SquashFS image containing game data is mounted at a specific path.

### Common Drive Options

A few options are shared across all builder types:

**`builder`** is required and determines how the drive is assembled. The available values are `"docker"`, `"directory"`, `"tar"`, `"none"`, and `"empty"`. Each builder is covered in its own section above.

**`mount`** controls where the drive is mounted inside the machine. It defaults to `/mnt/<name>`. You can set it to any absolute path. For example, `mount = "/var/lib/app"` makes the drive accessible at that path inside the machine.

**`shared`** when set to `true`, writes the changes the guest makes to the drive back to the drive's image file on the host, so they persist after the machine stops. When `false`, guest writes stay in the machine and the image file is left unchanged. Defaults to `false`.

**`user`** sets the Linux user that owns the files inside the drive. This matters when your application runs as a non-root user and needs read or write access to the drive's contents. Defaults to the user defined in the Docker image, or root if unset.

**`format`** determines the file system type. Choose `"ext2"` when your application needs to read and write to the drive, or `"sqfs"` for a compressed read only image. Not all builders support this option (the empty builder uses `"ext2"` or `"raw"`, and it's completely absent in the none builder).

**`extra_size`** adds free space beyond the actual content size. Useful for drives when you intend to convert to an ext2 format, it takes the actual size of the existing directory contents then adds the specified `extra_size` to it, allowing for future additions. Specified as a string like `"100Mb"` or `"50Mi"`.

## Putting It All Together: A Complete Example

Here is a realistic `cartesi.toml` for a Python application that processes uploaded documents. It has a root drive built from a Dockerfile, an empty drive for temporary storage, and a pre built drive containing reference data.

```toml
# Pin the SDK version for reproducible builds
# (0.12.0-alpha.45 ships rollups-node v2.0.0-alpha.14 and emulator 0.22.0)
sdk = "cartesi/sdk:0.12.0-alpha.45"

[machine]
# Run the Python application when the machine starts, through rollup-init,
# which starts the rollup HTTP server first. The Dockerfile copies the code
# into the root drive, at /opt/cartesi/dapp as in the Python template.
entrypoint = "rollup-init /usr/local/bin/python3 /opt/cartesi/dapp/dapp.py"

# Give the machine 256 megabytes of RAM for document processing
ram_length = "256Mi"

# Pull environment variables and working directory from the Docker image
use_docker_env = true
use_docker_workdir = true

# Run as the default non root user
user = "dapp"

# The root drive contains the OS, Python runtime, and application code
[drives.root]
builder = "docker"
dockerfile = "Dockerfile"
format = "ext2"
extra_size = "50Mb"

# An empty writable drive for temporary file processing
[drives.scratch]
builder = "empty"
size = "200Mb"
mount = "/tmp/processing"

# Pre built reference data that does not change between deployments
[drives.reference]
builder = "none"
filename = "./data/reference-corpus.sqfs"
mount = "/opt/data/reference"
```

In this setup:

The root drive is built from a Dockerfile that installs Python and copies in the application code. The `extra_size` gives it 50 megabytes of headroom for any files the OS or Python runtime might create.

The scratch drive is a 200 megabyte blank space where the application can write temporary files during document processing. Since it is empty, it starts fresh every time the machine boots.

The reference drive contains a pre built SquashFS image with static reference data. Because this data does not change, using SquashFS keeps the image small and read only.

## Quick Reference

| Field                   | Section      | Type             | Default                         | Description                                                     |
| ----------------------- | ------------ | ---------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sdk`                   | Top level    | String           | Default SDK of the CLI release  | SDK image and version used for building                         |
| `entrypoint`            | `[machine]`  | String           | From Docker image               | Path to the application binary                                  |
| `boot_args`             | `[machine]`  | String array     | CLI defaults                    | Linux kernel boot arguments                                     |
| `ram_length`            | `[machine]`  | String           | `"128Mi"`                       | Amount of RAM for the machine                                   |
| `ram_image`             | `[machine]`  | String           | SDK default                     | Path to the Linux kernel binary                                 |
| `max_mcycle`            | `[machine]`  | Number           | No limit                        | Maximum machine cycle of the boot run of `cartesi build`        |
| `assert_rolling_template` | `[machine]` | Boolean        | —                               | Fail the build if the machine is not a rolling template         |
| `use_docker_env`        | `[machine]`  | Boolean          | `true`                          | Inject Docker ENV into the machine                              |
| `use_docker_workdir`    | `[machine]`  | Boolean          | `true`                          | Use Docker WORKDIR in the machine                               |
| `user`                  | `[machine]`  | String           | `"dapp"`                        | User to run the application as                                  |
| `builder`               | `[drives.*]` | String           | `"docker"`                      | How to create the drive: docker, empty, directory, tar, or none |
| `dockerfile`            | `[drives.*]` | String           | `"Dockerfile"`                  | Path to Dockerfile (docker builder)                             |
| `target`                | `[drives.*]` | String           | Last stage                      | Docker multi stage build target                                 |
| `format`                | `[drives.*]` | String           | `"ext2"`                        | File system format: ext2 or sqfs (raw for the empty builder)    |
| `extra_size`            | `[drives.*]` | String           | `0`                             | Extra free space added to the drive                             |
| `size`                  | `[drives.*]` | String or Number | —                               | Total drive size (empty builder only)                           |
| `directory`             | `[drives.*]` | String           | —                               | Local directory to package (directory builder)                  |
| `filename`              | `[drives.*]` | String           | —                               | Path to tar or existing image file                              |
| `mount`                 | `[drives.*]` | String           | `/mnt/<name>`                   | Where the drive is mounted in the machine                       |
| `shared`                | `[drives.*]` | Boolean          | `false`                         | Write guest changes back to the drive's image file              |
| `user`                  | `[drives.*]` | String           | Docker image user               | Owner of the files inside the drive                             |
| `accounts_drive`        | `[drives.*]` | Boolean          | `false`                         | Mark the drive as the emergency-withdrawal accounts drive       |
| `accounts_drive_size`   | `[drives.*]` | String or Number | Whole drive                     | Size of the account tree inside the accounts drive              |

The CLI also accepts keys that this page does not cover: `env` and `env_file` in `[machine]`; `build_args`, `context`, `image` and `tags` for the docker builder; `format = "raw"` for the empty builder; and the `[nvrams]`, `[withdrawal]` and `[prt]` tables. For `accounts_drive`, `accounts_drive_size`, `mount = false` and `[withdrawal]`, see [Testing emergency withdrawal locally](./emergency-withdrawal/local-testing.md#configure-the-accounts-drive).

---
id: asset-handling
title: Asset handling
resources:
  - url: https://www.udemy.com/course/cartesi-masterclass/
    title: The Cartesi dApp Developer Free Course
---

Assets exist on the base layer, where they have actual meaning and value.

As with any execution layer solution, a Cartesi Application that wants to manipulate assets needs a secure way of "teleporting" the assets from the base layer to the execution layer and when necessary, back to the base layer.

Currently, Cartesi Rollups support the following types of assets:

- [Ether (ETH)](../api-reference/contracts/portals/EtherPortal.md)
- [ERC-20](../api-reference/contracts/portals/Erc20Portal.md)
- [ERC-721](../api-reference/contracts/portals/Erc721Portal.md)
- [ERC-1155 Single](../api-reference/contracts/portals/Erc1155SinglePortal.md)
- [ERC-1155 Batch](../api-reference/contracts/portals/Erc1155BatchPortal.md)

![img](../../..//static/img/v2.0/onchain-contracts.jpg)

## Deposits

Portals enable the safe transfer of assets from the base layer to the execution layer. Users authorize portals to deduct assets from their accounts and initiate transfers to the Application contract.

When an asset is deposited, it is on the base layer but gains a representation in the execution layer. The corresponding Portal contract sends an input via the application's `InputBox` contract (the one returned by the application's `getInputBox()` function) describing the type of asset, amount, and some data the depositor might want the application to read. The off-chain machine will then interpret and validate the input payload.

Deposit input payloads are always specified as packed ABI-encoded parameters, as detailed below.

![img](../../..//static/img/v2.0/deposit-payload.jpg)

### ABI encoding for deposits

| Asset             | Packed ABI-encoded payload fields                                                                                                                       | Standard ABI-encoded payload fields                                                                                              |
| :---------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Ether             | <ul><li>`address sender`,</li><li>`uint256 value`,</li><li>`bytes execLayerData`</li></ul>                                                              | none                                                                                                                             |
| ERC-20            | <ul><li>`address token`,</li><li>`address sender`,</li><li>`uint256 amount`,</li><li>`bytes execLayerData`</li></ul>                                    | none                                                                                                                             |
| ERC-721           | <ul><li>`address token`,</li><li>`address sender`,</li><li>`uint256 tokenId`,</li><li>standard ABI-encoded fields...</li></ul>                          | <ul><li>`bytes baseLayerData`,</li><li>`bytes execLayerData`</li></ul>                                                           |
| ERC-1155 (single) | <ul><li>`address token`,</li><li>`address sender`,</li><li>`uint256 tokenId`,</li><li>`uint256 value`,</li><li>standard ABI-encoded fields...</li></ul> | <ul><li>`bytes baseLayerData`,</li><li>`bytes execLayerData`</li></ul>                                                           |
| ERC-1155 (batch)  | <ul><li>`address token`,</li><li>`address sender`,</li><li>standard ABI-encoded fields...</li></ul>                                                     | <ul><li>`uint256[] tokenIds`,</li><li>`uint256[] values`,</li><li>`bytes baseLayerData`,</li><li>`bytes execLayerData`</li></ul> |

Refer to the functions provided below to understand how to handle asset deposits. When called inside your application's advance handler, these helpers decode the payload for the deposited asset type.

For example, to decode an ERC-20 deposit payload, you can use the following code snippets:

## Withdrawing assets

Users can deposit assets to a Cartesi Application, but only the Application can initiate withdrawals (the exception is [emergency withdrawal](./emergency-withdrawal/overview.md): after a foreclosure, users withdraw their balances directly on the base layer). When a withdrawal request is made, it’s processed and interpreted off-chain by the Cartesi Machine running the application’s code. Subsequently, the Cartesi Machine creates a voucher containing the necessary instructions for withdrawal, which becomes executable once the claim for the epoch that produced it has been accepted on-chain.

### Withdrawing Tokens

Vouchers are crucial in allowing applications in the execution layer to interact with contracts in the base layer through message calls. They are emitted by the off-chain machine and executed by any participant in the base layer. Each voucher includes a destination address and a payload, typically encoding a function call for Solidity contracts.

The application’s off-chain layer often requires knowledge of its address to facilitate on-chain interactions for withdrawals. To withdraw ERC-20 tokens that the application holds, the voucher calls `transfer(recipient, amount)` on the token contract: the Application contract makes the call, so the tokens leave its balance. Do not use `transferFrom(application, recipient, amount)` for this: the application has no allowance over its own tokens, so the call reverts with `ERC20InsufficientAllowance`.

Next, the off-chain machine uses the address of the application on the base layer to generate a voucher for execution at the executeOutput() function of the Application contract. This address is known to the offchain machine because it is embedded in the metadata of every input sent to the application, though the developer will need to implement extra logic to fetch this address from the metadata then properly store and retrieve it when needed in situations like generating the above Voucher.

Below are multi-language examples showing how to transfer tokens to whoever calls the application. The JavaScript example encodes the call with `viem`; add it as described in [adding dependencies](./creating-an-application.md#adding-dependencies-in-javascript-and-typescript). In each case, the encoded call data contains the token contract function and arguments (for example, recipient and amount). The voucher then includes a destination (the ERC-20 token contract), a payload (the encoded call data), and a value set to zero to indicate no Ether is sent with this transfer request.

### Withdrawing Ether

To execute Ether withdrawal it is important to emit a voucher with the necessary details as regarding whom you intend to send the Ether to and also the amount to send, nevertheless since the Application contract Executes vouchers by making a [safeCall](https://github.com/cartesi/rollups-contracts/blob/v3.0.0-alpha.10/src/library/LibAddress.sol#L20) to the destination, passing a value (Ether amount to send along with the call) and a payload (function signature to call), you should leave the payload empty (`0x`) if you do not intend to call any functions in the destination address while sending just the specified value of Ether to the destination address. If you intend to call a payable function and also send Ether along, you can add a function signature matching the payable function you intend to call to the payload field.

:::caution empty payload for wallets
A voucher with a non-empty payload reverts with `TargetHasNoCode` when its destination has no code, as is the case for a user's wallet (an externally owned account). Even a payload of zero bytes such as `0x0000...0000` counts as non-empty, so Ether withdrawals to wallets must use an empty payload.
:::

Below are multi-language examples for Ether withdrawal. Here, the voucher sends Ether directly to an address instead of calling a token contract function, so the payload is empty (`0x`) and the voucher's `value` field carries the amount in wei, as a `0x`-prefixed hex string.

:::note epoch length
The epoch length (in blocks) and the claim staging period are parameters of the application's consensus contract, fixed when the consensus is deployed; the node has no setting for them. `cartesi-rollups-cli deploy` uses an epoch length of 10 blocks and a claim staging period of 0 unless you pass `--epoch-length` and `--claim-staging-period`. `cartesi run` accepts the same two options, with defaults of 720 blocks and 0 (with the devnet's 2-second blocks, an epoch lasts about 24 minutes). A withdrawal voucher becomes executable only after its epoch closes and the claim is accepted, so these parameters set how long users wait for withdrawals.
:::

Here are the function signatures used by vouchers to withdraw the different types of assets:

| Asset    | Destination    | Function signature                                                                                                                          |
| :------- | :------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Ether    | Recipient      | None: empty payload (`0x`), with the amount in the voucher's `value` field                                                                 |
| ERC-20   | Token contract | `transfer(address,uint256)` [:page_facing_up:](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20#methods)                                               |
| ERC-721  | Token contract | `safeTransferFrom(address,address,uint256)` [:page_facing_up:](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-721#specification)                        |
| ERC-721  | Token contract | `safeTransferFrom(address,address,uint256,bytes)` [:page_facing_up:](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-721#specification)                  |
| ERC-1155 | Token contract | `safeTransferFrom(address,address,uint256,uint256,bytes)` [:page_facing_up:](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155#specification)         |
| ERC-1155 | Token contract | `safeBatchTransferFrom(address,address,uint256[],uint256[],bytes)` [:page_facing_up:](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155#specification) |

---
id: building-an-application
title: Building an application
---

“Building” in this context compiles your application into RISC-V architecture and consequently builds a Cartesi machine containing your application. This architecture enables computation done by your application to be reproducible and verifiable.

Ensure you have Docker engine running, then navigate the directory to your application and build by running:

```shell
cartesi build
```

The successful execution of this step logs output like the following, from a template that uses the rollup HTTP server (Python, Rust, Go or C++). The JavaScript and TypeScript templates do not start the rollup HTTP server, so their build log has no `rollup_http_server` lines:

```shell

         .
        / \
      /    \
\---/---\  /----\
 \       X       \
  \----/  \---/---\
       \    / CARTESI
        \ /   MACHINE
         '

[INFO  rollup_http_server] starting http dispatcher service...
[INFO  rollup_http_server::http_service] starting http dispatcher http service!
[INFO  actix_server::builder] starting 1 workers
[INFO  actix_server::server] Actix runtime found; starting in Actix runtime
[INFO  rollup_http_server::dapp_process] starting dapp: dapp
Sending finish

Manual yield rx-accepted (1) (0x000020 data)
Cycles: 69709199
69709199: 9e0420c0fda1a5dc9256b3f9783b09f207e5222a88429e91629cc2e495282b35
Storing machine: please wait
```

## Memory

To change the default memory size for the Cartesi Machine, set `ram_length` in the `[machine]` section of a `cartesi.toml` file in your project's root (see [advanced configuration](./advanced-configuration.md#memory-settings)).

The lines below set the memory size to 128 mebibytes, which is the default:

```toml
[machine]
ram_length = "128Mi"
```

:::note environment variables
To override a variable that controls the rollups-node started by `cartesi run`, export it in your shell before running the command. Only the variables listed by `cartesi run --list-supported-variables` are passed to the node.
:::

<!-- source: https://docs.cartesi.io/cartesi-rollups/2.0/development/creating-an-application/ -->

---
id: creating-an-application
title: Creating an Application
resources:
  - url: https://cartesiscan.io/
    title: CartesiScan
---



Cartesi CLI simplifies creating applications on Cartesi. To create a new application, run:

```shell
cartesi create <application-name> --template <language>
```

For example, create a JavaScript project.

```shell
cartesi create new-app --template javascript
```

This command creates a `new-app` directory with essential files for your application development.

- `Dockerfile`: Contains configurations to build a complete Cartesi machine with your app's dependencies. Your backend code will run in this environment.

- `README.md`: A markdown file with basic information and instructions about your application.

- `src/index.js`: A JavaScript file with template backend code that serves as your application's entry point.

- `package.json`: A list of dependencies required for your application along with the name, version and description of your application.

- `pnpm-lock.yaml` and `pnpm-workspace.yaml`: The [pnpm](https://pnpm.io) lockfile and settings. The template manages its packages with pnpm, in the version pinned by the `packageManager` field of `package.json`, through [corepack](https://nodejs.org/api/corepack.html): run `corepack enable pnpm` once if the `pnpm` command is not available.

- `rolldown.config.js`: The [rolldown](https://rolldown.rs) configuration that bundles `src/index.js` into `dist/index.mjs`, the file the Cartesi Machine runs.

The TypeScript template has the same layout, with `src/index.ts`, `rolldown.config.ts` and a `tsconfig.json`.

Cartesi CLI has templates for the following languages – `cpp`, `cpp-low-level`, `go`, `java`, `javascript`, `lua`, `python`, `ruby`, `rust`, and `typescript`.

:::note Libraries for simplifying development
High-level frameworks can simplify routing, inputs, and testing. For TypeScript use Deroll; for Python use python-Cartesi or Cartesapp.
See [Community tools](../resources/community-tools.md).
:::

## Implementing your application Logic

After creating your application, you can begin building your application by adding your logic to the index.js file. This file serves as the entry point of your application. While your project can include multiple files and directories, the default application file should remain the entry point of your application.

It’s important not to modify or remove existing code in index.js unless you fully understand its purpose, as doing so may prevent your application from functioning correctly. Instead, you are encouraged to extend the file by adding your own logic and implementations alongside the default code.

The default application templates include two primary handlers, one for each type of request. In most templates, they are the `handle_advance` and `handle_inspect` functions. In the JavaScript and TypeScript templates, they are the `advance` and `inspect` handlers passed to `rollup.run()` from the [`@cartesi/rollup`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@cartesi/rollup/v/1.0.0-alpha.3) package, which talks directly to the Cartesi Machine instead of going through the rollup HTTP server: each handler receives the request, with its `payload` as a Node.js `Buffer`, and emits outputs with `rollup.emitNotice()`, `rollup.emitVoucher()` and `rollup.emitReport()`.

### handle_advance function

The `handle_advance` function (the `advance` handler in JavaScript and TypeScript) is the entry point for state modifying logic, you can think of this like handling "write" requests in traditional web context. It is intended to carry out computations, updates, and other logic that changes the state of the application. Where appropriate, it can emit outputs such as `notices`, `vouchers`, or `reports`. In JavaScript and TypeScript, the handler accepts the input unless it returns `false`.

### handle_inspect function

On the other hand, the `handle_inspect` function (the `inspect` handler in JavaScript and TypeScript) serves as the entry point for read only operations, similar to "read" requests in a typical web context. This function should be implemented to accept user input, perform any necessary lookups or calculations based on the current state, and return the results by emitting a `report`. It's important to understand that handle_inspect is designed strictly for reading the application's state, it should not perform any modifications.

### Adding dependencies in JavaScript and TypeScript

`cartesi build` installs the packages listed under `dependencies` in `package.json` inside an emulated RISC-V container, where pnpm can crash with a segmentation fault while it installs a large package such as `viem`. Add pure JavaScript packages as development dependencies instead, pinned to an exact version, and let rolldown bundle them into your application:

```shell
pnpm add -D viem@2.57.19
```

Then, in `rolldown.config.js` (`rolldown.config.ts` in the TypeScript template), leave only the native addon out of the bundle:

```javascript
  external: ["@cartesi/rollup"],
```

`@cartesi/rollup` is a native addon: it stays under `dependencies`, and the build installs its prebuilt RISC-V binary in the machine. The template's lockfile pins it to `1.0.0-alpha.3`; if you add it to a project yourself, pin that version too (`pnpm add @cartesi/rollup@1.0.0-alpha.3`), because its `latest` npm tag points to an older `0.0.0` release. A package that ships a native addon of its own cannot be bundled either: keep it under `dependencies` and add it to `external`.

## Implementing Outputs

If your application needs to emit Outputs like; notices, vouchers, or reports, make sure to implement the corresponding logic within your codebase to properly handle these outputs. You can check out the respective pages for [Notice](../api-reference/backend/notices.md), [Vouchers](../api-reference/backend/vouchers.md) or [Report](../api-reference/backend/reports.md) for better understanding of what they are and how to implement them.

For your application you'll need to include your personal logic and also emit outputs when necessary. ---
id: installation-Guide
title: Installing the required tools
---

The [Emergency Withdrawal Recovery Guide](./recovery-guide.md) runs its tools directly on your machine. This is convenient on a local devnet, where you interact with them directly rather than through the node's containers. This page installs everything you need for [Cartesi Rollups Node v2.0.0-alpha.14](https://github.com/cartesi/rollups-node/releases/tag/v2.0.0-alpha.14). Each tool below has a short description, followed by Linux and then macOS steps.

## Cartesi Machine emulator

The Cartesi Machine is the deterministic RISC-V virtual machine your application runs in. The machine tool spawns it to reproduce the settled state and generate the withdrawal proofs, so the emulator must be installed.

Install the emulator version your Cartesi Rollups Node release was built with. Node v2.0.0-alpha.14 requires emulator **0.22.x** (it is built against 0.22.0). This is also the version the application's machine template must have been built with: emulator 0.22 changed every machine state hash, so an emulator from another version line cannot reproduce the application's settled state.

### Linux (Debian or Ubuntu)

Download the emulator package for your architecture from the [v0.22.0 release](https://github.com/cartesi/machine-emulator/releases/tag/v0.22.0) and install it (this also installs its dependencies, including `lua5.4`):

```sh
ARCH=$(dpkg --print-architecture)   # amd64 or arm64
wget https://github.com/cartesi/machine-emulator/releases/download/v0.22.0/machine-emulator_${ARCH}.deb
sudo apt-get install ./machine-emulator_${ARCH}.deb
```

### macOS

Install with Homebrew:

```sh
brew install cartesi/tap/cartesi-machine
cartesi-machine --version
```

Homebrew always installs the tap's current emulator release and cannot install an older version of this formula. The tap ships 0.22.0 since [this formula revision](https://github.com/cartesi/homebrew-tap/blob/aef3af203d5bb93a803402dfad0008bf9f96f00b/Formula/cartesi-machine.rb). If `cartesi-machine --version` reports a version other than 0.22.x, uninstall it (`brew uninstall cartesi-machine cartesi-machine-emulator`) and build v0.22.0 from source as described below.

If a package is not available for your system, build the emulator from source following the [Cartesi Machine v0.22.0 build instructions](https://github.com/cartesi/machine-emulator/tree/v0.22.0#from-sources).

## Cartesi Rollups Node tools

The recovery flow uses two command-line tools that ship together with the Cartesi Rollups Node:

- **`cartesi-rollups-cli`** sends the on-chain transactions (foreclose, anchor the drive root, withdraw) and reads withdrawals;
- **`cartesi-rollups-machine-tool`** reproduces the settled machine state (`replay`) and generates the accounts-drive proofs (`prove accounts-drive`).

The node releases publish prebuilt packages only as Debian `.deb` files (amd64 and arm64). On macOS, and on other systems, you build the tools from source.

### Linux (Debian or Ubuntu, amd64 or arm64)

Download the node package for your architecture from the [Cartesi Rollups Node v2.0.0-alpha.14 release](https://github.com/cartesi/rollups-node/releases/tag/v2.0.0-alpha.14) and install it (this installs all node binaries, including both tools). The package requires the 0.22 emulator installed above:

```sh
ARCH=$(dpkg --print-architecture)   # amd64 or arm64
wget https://github.com/cartesi/rollups-node/releases/download/v2.0.0-alpha.14/cartesi-rollups-node-v2.0.0-alpha.14_${ARCH}.deb
sudo apt-get install ./cartesi-rollups-node-v2.0.0-alpha.14_${ARCH}.deb
```

To install only the two tools, extract them from the downloaded package instead of installing it:

```sh
dpkg-deb -x cartesi-rollups-node-v2.0.0-alpha.14_${ARCH}.deb out/
sudo cp out/usr/bin/cartesi-rollups-cli out/usr/bin/cartesi-rollups-machine-tool /usr/local/bin/
```

### macOS

Build the tools from source. You need Go >= 1.27.3 and GNU Make >= 3.81. Install Go with Homebrew (macOS already ships GNU Make 3.81):

```sh
brew install go
```

Then clone the release tag and build only the two tools. Both are pure Go programs, so this step does not link against the emulator library:

```sh
git clone --branch v2.0.0-alpha.14 https://github.com/cartesi/rollups-node.git
cd rollups-node
make cartesi-rollups-cli cartesi-rollups-machine-tool
sudo install -m 0755 cartesi-rollups-cli cartesi-rollups-machine-tool /usr/local/bin/
```

Make sure `/usr/local/bin` is on your `PATH`. The machine tool still runs the `cartesi-machine` emulator installed above.

## Lua 5.4 (PRT applications only)

For an application that uses PRT (Dave) consensus, `cartesi-rollups-machine-tool replay` runs a Lua script. It needs Lua 5.4 and the emulator's Lua modules:

- **Lua 5.4.** The tool runs `lua5.4` by default; pass another executable with `--lua`. On Linux, the emulator package above already installed `lua5.4`. On macOS, Homebrew installs Lua 5.4 as a dependency of the emulator (`lua@5.4`) but does not put it on your `PATH`, so pass it explicitly: `--lua "$(brew --prefix lua@5.4)/bin/lua5.4"`.
- **The emulator's Lua modules.** The tool finds them from the `cartesi-machine` installation. If replay cannot load the `cartesi` Lua module, pass `--cartesi-sdk-root` with the emulator's installation prefix (the directory that contains `share/lua/5.4`).

## Verify

```sh
cartesi-machine --version          # 0.22.x
cartesi-rollups-cli --version      # 2.0.0-alpha.14
cartesi-rollups-machine-tool --help
```

Once these run, continue with the [Emergency Withdrawal Recovery Guide](./recovery-guide.md).

<!-- source: https://docs.cartesi.io/cartesi-rollups/2.0/development/emergency-withdrawal/lifecycle/ -->

---
id: lifecycle
title: Claim & Foreclosure Lifecycle
---

To understand foreclosure, it helps to first see how an application's inputs turn into settled state, and where foreclosure fits in. This page walks through that lifecycle.

## From inputs to a settled claim

**Inputs.** A user action (a deposit through a portal, or a message sent to the app) becomes an **input**, recorded on-chain in the [`InputBox`](../../api-reference/contracts/input-box.md).

**Epochs.** Inputs are not settled one at a time. They are grouped into **epochs**: batches of consecutive inputs that are settled together as a single claim. Every input belongs to exactly one epoch. How epoch boundaries are drawn depends on the consensus; under Authority and Quorum an epoch covers a range of blocks, set by the consensus `epochLength`. Under PRT (Dave), a new epoch is sealed each time the previous epoch's result is accepted, and it holds every input added since the previous epoch was sealed.

**Claims.** The application runs as a deterministic Cartesi Machine. The node feeds each input to the machine as it arrives, advancing the machine's state and producing outputs. When the epoch closes, the node reduces the resulting state to a single fingerprint, a **claim** (a Merkle root), and posts it on-chain so the consensus contract can trust the off-chain computation by verifying one hash.

Under Authority and Quorum, posting a claim happens in **two transactions**:

1. **Submit** (`submitClaim`) posts the claim. The node marks the epoch `CLAIM_SUBMITTED` when it sends the transaction, and `CLAIM_STAGED` once the claim is staged on-chain. Under Authority, submitting the claim stages it; under Quorum, the claim is staged when a majority of the validators has submitted it.
2. **Accept** (`acceptClaim`) finalizes it, once a waiting period has passed. The epoch becomes `CLAIM_ACCEPTED`.

The waiting period between the two is the **claim staging period**, measured in blocks and fixed when the consensus is deployed. The consensus contract enforces it: `acceptClaim` reverts until enough blocks have passed since the claim was staged. A staging period of `0` lets a claim be accepted in the same block in which it is staged.

**Under PRT (Dave),** validators do not vote on a claim: each epoch is settled by a dispute tournament on the `DaveConsensus` contract. Once the tournament has a winner, anyone can call `stageTournamentResult`. It only accepts a winning post-epoch machine state that comes with a proof that the machine finished the epoch ready for the next input (a manual yield with an "rx accepted" reason). `acceptStagedTournamentResult` can then finalize the result once either the claim staging period has passed since staging, or every sentry configured in the consensus has submitted a claim for the same post-epoch state. A sentry node submits the post-epoch state it computed itself, so sentries can shorten the wait only for a result they agree with. A consensus without sentries always waits for the staging period.

## The epoch status flow

An epoch moves through these statuses:

![Epoch status flow: OPEN to INPUTS_PROCESSED to CLAIM_COMPUTED to CLAIM_STAGED to CLAIM_ACCEPTED, with a foreclosure branch diverting an unfinalized claim to CLAIM_FORECLOSED](../../epoch-flow.png)

The diagram leaves out the transient `CLOSED` and `CLAIM_SUBMITTED` statuses, which the list below includes.

- **OPEN**: the epoch's block range is still current and collecting inputs.
- **CLOSED**: the epoch has closed (its block range ended or, under PRT, it was sealed on-chain), but the machine has not yet processed all of its inputs.
- **INPUTS_PROCESSED**: the epoch has closed and the machine has processed all of its inputs.
- **CLAIM_COMPUTED**: the node has the claim ready.
- **CLAIM_SUBMITTED**: the node has sent the claim transaction and is waiting to see the claim staged on-chain.
- **CLAIM_STAGED**: the claim was submitted on-chain and is in its staging window.
- **CLAIM_ACCEPTED**: the staging period elapsed and the claim was finalized. This is the settled state that outputs (and emergency withdrawal) rely on.
- **CLAIM_FORECLOSED**: a terminal status a claim reaches if the application is foreclosed before that claim finalizes (see below).
- **CLAIM_REJECTED**: this is a related terminal status, but a **node-level** one rather than an on-chain outcome. The node marks its own epoch `CLAIM_REJECTED` (and the application `DIVERGED`) when it observes that a claim different from the one it computed was accepted on-chain, for example on a Quorum where another validator's claim won the vote. 

## Foreclosure

Everything above assumes the operator keeps running the node and the application operates in optimum condition. Foreclosure is what happens when you can no longer depend on that. 

**Foreclosure** is the act of permanently freezing a Cartesi Rollups application at its last accepted state, this process can be triggered in situations where the operator abandons the application, a bug is discovered in the application code, a compromised authority, a dishonest quorum majority, a false claim is left unchallenged in a PRT dispute tournament, or a PRT epoch cannot be settled at all (see [Epochs that PRT cannot settle](#epochs-that-prt-cannot-settle)). 

The claim staging period is the guardian's window to act: foreclosing before such a claim is accepted terminalizes it as `CLAIM_FORECLOSED` and freezes the application on the last state it still trusts, so users withdraw against that state and not the bad one. Note that foreclosure does not reverse a claim that has already been accepted; once a state is accepted it is what emergency withdrawals pay out from, which is why the guardian's protection depends on acting within the staging window.

Choose the staging period with this in mind: it must cover the guardian's reaction time, in blocks, from noticing a bad claim to getting `foreclose()` included on-chain. A staging period of `0` gives the guardian no window at all, because a claim can be staged and accepted in the same block. `cartesi-rollups-cli deploy` uses `0` unless you pass `--claim-staging-period` (see [Deploying with emergency withdrawal](../../deployment/self-hosted/with-emergency-withdrawal.md)). Under PRT, a staged result can also be accepted before the staging period ends once every sentry has submitted a matching claim, so with sentries the guardian's window can be shorter, down to zero blocks.

To foreclose an application, the **guardian**, a single address fixed in the withdrawal config, calls [`foreclose()`](../../api-reference/contracts/application.md#foreclose) on the application contract.  [`isForeclosed()`](../../api-reference/contracts/application.md#isforeclosed) becomes `true` and this permanently freezes the application:

**A foreclosed application can no longer process inputs.** Once frozen it takes on no new inputs (the `InputBox` rejects them) and settles no new state. What remains is returning the assets users already deposited, directly from the contracts:

- [emergency withdrawal](./recovery-guide.md) pays out the balances in the accounts drive of the last settled state;
- [deposit refunds](./recovery-guide.md#step-7-refund-unfinalized-deposits) return portal deposits whose inputs were never finalized, through [`issueRefund()`](../../api-reference/contracts/application.md#issuerefund). Refunds are not automatic: anyone can send them, but someone has to;
- outputs, such as vouchers, of epochs accepted before the foreclosure can still be executed as usual.

Foreclosure is a property of the **application contract** and of the **node**. It takes both to make the freeze permanent:

- **The contract** holds the on-chain truth. `foreclose()` can only be called by the guardian, only once (a second call reverts with `Foreclosed()`), and sets `isForeclosed()`, after which the normal `submitClaim` and `acceptClaim` paths revert. Under PRT, `DaveConsensus` likewise rejects staging, acceptance, sentry claims, and sentry rotation. The contract also gates emergency withdrawal and refunds so those paths only open once the application is foreclosed.
- **The node** observes that truth and acts on it. Its EVM Reader detects the on-chain `Foreclosure` event, records it in the node database, and stops reading inputs for that application at the foreclosure block, so the node no longer claims new inputs; however it still keeps watching the base layer so as to index subsequent emergency withdrawals. The node does not index refunds (`RefundIssued`), and it does not generate the withdrawal proofs: the separate `cartesi-rollups-machine-tool` does, from the inputs in a node database (see [After foreclosure](#after-foreclosure-prove-and-withdraw)).

![Foreclosure sequence: the guardian calls foreclose() on the application contract; the node's EVM Reader observes isForeclosed(), records the foreclosure in its database, then continues its scanners to drain pre-foreclosure inputs and index post-foreclosure events](../../foreclosure-sequence.png)

Foreclosure has three effects on claims:

- **Accepted history is kept.** An epoch that already reached `CLAIM_ACCEPTED` stays accepted. Foreclosure does not rewrite settled history.
- **In-flight claims are cancelled.** A claim that has not finalized cannot finalize once the operator's authority is frozen, so the node marks it terminal as `CLAIM_FORECLOSED` instead of leaving it stuck. This happens whether the claim was still pre-staging (`CLAIM_COMPUTED` or `CLAIM_SUBMITTED`) or already `CLAIM_STAGED`. Under PRT, a staged result that was not accepted is never accepted, and the inputs of its epoch stay unfinalized, which is what makes their deposits refundable.
- **The state is frozen.** The application settles at its last accepted epoch, a final state that anyone with the application's inputs can reproduce on their own.

## Epochs that PRT cannot settle

Under PRT, some epochs can never be staged, so they never settle:

- the tournament ends without a winner;
- the application is terminal: on some input the machine halted or yielded with an exception, so the post-epoch state cannot pass the proof `stageTournamentResult` requires;
- the winning post-epoch state cannot pass that proof for any other reason.

The application then stops making progress: the stuck epoch is never accepted, so no later epoch is sealed and nothing new settles. The way out is foreclosure. The guardian forecloses, withdrawals use the last state that was accepted, and the deposits of the stuck epoch can be refunded. An application deployed without a guardian cannot be foreclosed, so in this situation it has no on-chain recovery at all: no withdrawals and no refunds.

The terminal-application case is not specific to PRT. Under Authority and Quorum, `submitClaim` requires the same proof about the post-epoch machine, so the claim of an epoch in which the application became terminal cannot be submitted either, and foreclosure is again the way out.

Foreclosure only stops settlement. The tournament contracts do not check foreclosure, so running tournaments can still be played to the end, and bonds can still be recovered from them. Off-chain, the PRT nodes react differently:

- The PRT service of the Cartesi Rollups Node (`cartesi-rollups-prt`, [v2.0.0-alpha.14](https://github.com/cartesi/rollups-node/tree/v2.0.0-alpha.14/internal/prt)) detects the foreclosure, stops joining tournaments and staging or accepting results for that application, and marks the pending epochs that can no longer be accepted as `CLAIM_FORECLOSED`.
- The node in the Dave repository ([v3.0.0-alpha.6](https://github.com/cartesi/dave/tree/v3.0.0-alpha.6/cartesi-rollups/node)) does not check whether the application is foreclosed: the settlement transactions it plans revert, and it keeps retrying them and logging errors. Its [README](https://github.com/cartesi/dave/tree/v3.0.0-alpha.6/cartesi-rollups/node/README.md) advises letting it finish recovering its winning bonds after a foreclosure, and then stopping it.

## After foreclosure: prove and withdraw

Once frozen, the accounts drive (the in-app balance ledger inside the machine state) at the last accepted epoch is the source of truth for balances. The contract proves the drive against the last finalized machine root, which the application reads from its consensus with `getLastFinalizedMachineMerkleRoot()`:

- **Authority and Quorum**: the machine root of the latest accepted claim.
- **PRT (`DaveConsensus`)**: the post-epoch machine state of the latest accepted tournament result.
- **No epoch accepted yet**: the consensus returns zero, and the application uses its template hash, the initial machine state, instead. The balances are then those of the template, normally none, and deposits are recovered through refunds.

Turning that into on-chain payouts takes three steps, one off-chain and two on-chain:

1. **Generate the proofs.** Off-chain, anyone runs the **machine tool** (`cartesi-rollups-machine-tool`) to replay the settled machine state and then `prove accounts-drive`. Replay is deterministic, so anyone can reproduce the last accepted state independently. It needs the application's inputs, which it reads from a Cartesi Rollups Node database: if the operator's node is gone, run your own node as a reader (see the [recovery guide](./recovery-guide.md#before-you-start)). Only the on-chain steps below need no node. This writes two proof files: `drive-root-proof.json` (the accounts-drive root and its proof against the machine state, used once in step 2) and `account-proof.json` (the per-account Merkle proofs, used in step 3).
2. **Anchor the ledger.** Anyone calls [`proveAccountsDriveMerkleRoot()`](../../api-reference/contracts/application.md#proveaccountsdrivemerkleroot) once, passing the root and proof from `drive-root-proof.json`. The contract checks it against the settled machine state and stores it. This is permissionless and happens once per application.
3. **Withdraw per account.** Each account is withdrawn with [`withdraw()`](../../api-reference/contracts/application.md#withdraw), passing the account and its Merkle proof from `account-proof.json`. The contract validates the account against the anchored root, builds a transfer output, marks the account as withdrawn so it cannot be withdrawn twice, and then runs the output. The gas payer can differ from the recipient.

As each on-chain step lands, the node's EVM Reader indexes it: it records the `AccountsDriveMerkleRootProved` event when the ledger is anchored, and stores each `Withdrawal` event (keyed by application and account index) so clients can read withdrawals over JSON-RPC and the CLI. Refunds are not indexed by the node: check them on-chain with `wasRefundForInputIssued()`.

![Accounts-drive proof and withdrawal sequence: the machine tool produces drive-root-proof.json and account-proof.json; the operator calls proveAccountsDriveMerkleRoot() then withdraw() on the application contract; the node's EVM Reader indexes the AccountsDriveMerkleRootProved and Withdrawal events](../../accounts-drive-withdrawal.png)

<!-- source: https://docs.cartesi.io/cartesi-rollups/2.0/development/emergency-withdrawal/local-testing/ -->

---
id: local-testing
title: Testing emergency withdrawal locally with cartesi run
---

The [recovery guide](./recovery-guide.md) runs the node tools on your own machine, against any chain. To try the whole flow on a local devnet first, you do not need to install anything beyond the Cartesi CLI: `cartesi run` deploys the application with a withdrawal config derived from its accounts drive, and three CLI commands run the recovery for you inside the devnet's node container:

- `cartesi foreclose` forecloses the application, signing as its guardian;
- `cartesi withdraw` replays the application up to its last finalized epoch, generates the accounts-drive proofs, anchors the accounts-drive root on-chain the first time, and withdraws an account's balance;
- `cartesi refund <input-index>` refunds a portal deposit that was not finalized before the foreclosure.

You need Cartesi CLI 2.0.0-alpha.42 or later (it defaults to the SDK with Cartesi Rollups Node v2.0.0-alpha.14), and an application that keeps its balances in an accounts drive, in the layout described in [Emergency Withdrawal (guest requirements)](../../api-reference/backend/emergency-withdrawal.md). The `cast` and `curl` commands used to check the results need [Foundry](https://getfoundry.sh) and `jq`.

The example on this page is a ledger application written in Python. It uses the single-asset ledger of [machine-asset-tools](https://github.com/Mugen-Builders/machine-asset-tools/tree/v0.1.0-alpha.11) v0.1.0-alpha.11 to credit ERC-20 deposits of the devnet `TestUsdc` token to its accounts drive. It opens the ledger on the whole 4 MiB drive (`/dev/pmem1`) with room for 4096 accounts:

```python
ACCOUNTS_DEVICE = environ.get("ACCOUNTS_DEVICE", "/dev/pmem1")
DRIVE_SIZE = 4 * 1024 * 1024  # [drives.accounts] size
N_ACCOUNTS = 1 << 12  # log2MaxNumOfAccounts = 12
...
check(
    lib.cma_ledger_init_single_file(
        ledger,
        ACCOUNTS_DEVICE.encode(),
        ctypes.c_size_t(0),
        ctypes.c_size_t(DRIVE_SIZE),
        ctypes.c_size_t(N_ACCOUNTS),
        ctypes.c_int(CMA_LEDGER_ASSET_TYPE_TOKEN_ADDRESS),
        token,  # the devnet TestUsdc address
    ),
    "cma_ledger_init_single_file",
)
```

The ledger writes the 4096 balance records, 32 bytes each, at the beginning of the drive (the first 128 KiB), and keeps its own bookkeeping after them. This matters for the configuration below.

## Configure the accounts drive

Mark the accounts drive in `cartesi.toml` with `accounts_drive = true`. The CLI then derives the application's [`WithdrawalConfig`](../../api-reference/contracts/withdrawal/withdrawal-config.md) from the built machine, so you never compute `accountsDriveStartIndex` or `log2MaxNumOfAccounts` yourself:

```toml
# SDK image for rollups-node v2.0.0-alpha.14 (Cartesi Machine emulator 0.22.0).
sdk = "cartesi/sdk:0.12.0-alpha.45"

# The application and OS, built from your Dockerfile.
[drives.root]
builder = "docker"
dockerfile = "Dockerfile"
format = "ext2"

# The accounts drive: a raw, unformatted flash drive for the balance ledger.
[drives.accounts]
builder = "empty"
format = "raw"
size = 4194304                 # 4 MiB, the whole file the ledger library manages
mount = false
user = "dapp"
accounts_drive = true          # derive the withdrawal config from this drive
accounts_drive_size = "128Ki"  # only the balance records: 4096 accounts x 32 bytes

# Optional. Without this table, cartesi run uses the devnet values shown here.
# [withdrawal]
# guardian = "0x70997970C51812dc3A010C7d01b50e0d17dc79C8"                   # devnet account 1
# withdrawal_output_builder = "0xB4D253c7a110241561B3eD6d632846dF7d4e9Af7"  # devnet TestUsdWithdrawalOutputBuilder
# account_size = 32                                                         # bytes per account
```

- `accounts_drive = true` marks the drive that holds the accounts. Only one can be marked, and it must be `builder = "empty"`, `format = "raw"` and not mounted.
- `accounts_drive_size` limits the accounts drive to the beginning of a larger drive. Leave it out only if your balance records fill the whole drive. It must be a power of two, no larger than the drive.
- `[withdrawal]` is optional. Each key overrides one value:

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|-----|---------|---------|
| `guardian` | `0x70997970C51812dc3A010C7d01b50e0d17dc79C8` (devnet account 1) | The only address allowed to foreclose. |
| `withdrawal_output_builder` | `0xB4D253c7a110241561B3eD6d632846dF7d4e9Af7` (devnet `TestUsdWithdrawalOutputBuilder`) | Decodes an account and builds its payout. The devnet builder pays out `TestUsdc` (`0x7a051EDffC0884cd88d4a377F4C87BE074CF6c81`) and expects 32-byte accounts. |
| `account_size` | `32` | Bytes per account, a power of two of at least 32. Gives `log2LeavesPerAccount`. |

The default guardian and builder exist only on the `cartesi run` devnet. Against a fork of another chain the CLI requires `withdrawal_output_builder`, since the devnet builder is not deployed there.

:::caution Size the accounts drive to the records, not to the file
`log2MaxNumOfAccounts` comes from the size of the accounts drive, and it is fixed on-chain at deployment. If the ledger keeps other data after its records, as the machine-asset-tools ledger does, and you leave out `accounts_drive_size`, the application deploys with a geometry that covers that data too (`log2_max_num_of_accounts` 17 for this 4 MiB drive, instead of 12). Nothing fails until the recovery: `cartesi withdraw` then stops with `account 4096 appears after the first empty slot`, and since the deposits were finalized, they cannot be refunded either. Set `accounts_drive_size` to the number of accounts the ledger was opened with, times the account size.
:::

## Build

`cartesi build` builds the machine, finds where the emulator placed the accounts drive, and prints the configuration it derives:

```sh
cartesi build
```

```text
...
Storing machine: please wait

accounts drive  accounts (flash drive) → /dev/pmem1
start           0xa0000000
size            128 KiB (2^17 bytes), at the beginning of 4 MiB
accounts        4096 × 32 bytes

withdrawal config
  guardian                    0x70997970C51812dc3A010C7d01b50e0d17dc79C8  devnet account 1
  withdrawal_output_builder   0xB4D253c7a110241561B3eD6d632846dF7d4e9Af7  devnet TestUsdWithdrawalOutputBuilder
  account_size                32 bytes                                    default
  log2_leaves_per_account     0                                           derived
  log2_max_num_of_accounts    12                                          derived
  accounts_drive_start_index  20480 (0x5000)                              derived

--withdrawal-config '{"guardian":"0x70997970C51812dc3A010C7d01b50e0d17dc79C8","log2_leaves_per_account":0,"log2_max_num_of_accounts":12,"accounts_drive_start_index":20480,"withdrawal_output_builder":"0xB4D253c7a110241561B3eD6d632846dF7d4e9Af7"}'
devnet defaults in use: set guardian and withdrawal_output_builder under [withdrawal] to deploy elsewhere
```

The first line names the device the guest opens the drive at (`/dev/pmem1` here). `accounts_drive_start_index` is the drive's start address divided by the accounts-drive size (`0xa0000000 / 0x20000 = 0x5000`). The `--withdrawal-config` line is the value `cartesi run` passes to the node's `cartesi-rollups-cli deploy application`; use the same value to deploy this machine yourself ([Deploying with emergency withdrawal](../../deployment/self-hosted/with-emergency-withdrawal.md)), after setting your own `guardian` and `withdrawal_output_builder`.

Without `accounts_drive = true`, `cartesi build` prints no withdrawal section, and `cartesi run` deploys the application without a withdrawal config: its guardian is the zero address and it can never be foreclosed.

## Run the devnet

The `cartesi` commands on this page find the devnet and the application by the project name, which defaults to the name of the current directory. The output and the JSON-RPC calls below assume the project directory is named `ewapp`: run every command from that directory, or replace `ewapp` with your directory's name.

Start the devnet and keep it running in its own terminal:

```sh
cartesi run --epoch-length 10 --claim-staging-period 30 --port 6791
```

```text
WARNING: default block is set to 'latest', production configuration will likely use 'finalized'
✔ ewapp starting at http://127.0.0.1:6791
❯ anvil service starting...
❯ rpc service starting...
❯ inspect service starting...
✔ anvil service ready at http://127.0.0.1:6791/anvil
✔ inspect service ready at http://127.0.0.1:6791/inspect/ewapp
✔ rpc service ready at http://127.0.0.1:6791/rpc
✔ ewapp machine hash is 0x5ab71fe4c8acee6dd863c186f7d88b2e67569df7bc91255f04eec4b40571e907
✔ ewapp contract deployed at 0x19607994febf8381df4be89cd82cdd984285c7c0
```

- `--epoch-length 10` closes an epoch every 10 blocks (20 seconds at the default 2-second block time), instead of every 720 blocks.
- `--claim-staging-period 30` keeps each claim staged for 30 blocks (about 60 seconds) before it can be accepted. This is the guardian's window: a deposit whose epoch is still open or staged when you foreclose is never finalized, and is returned by a refund. With the default of `0`, a claim is accepted as soon as it is staged, so only deposits whose epoch has not been claimed yet stay unfinalized.
- `--port 6791` fixes the devnet's address for the `cast` and `curl` commands below.

`cartesi run` derives the same withdrawal config from the built machine and deploys with it, but does not print it. Check what was deployed on-chain, with the address printed above:

```sh
RPC=http://127.0.0.1:6791/anvil
APP=0x19607994febf8381df4be89cd82cdd984285c7c0
```

```sh
for f in 'getGuardian()(address)' 'getWithdrawalOutputBuilder()(address)' \
         'getLog2LeavesPerAccount()(uint8)' 'getLog2MaxNumOfAccounts()(uint8)' \
         'getAccountsDriveStartIndex()(uint64)'; do
  cast call $APP "$f" --rpc-url $RPC
done
```

```text
0x70997970C51812dc3A010C7d01b50e0d17dc79C8
0xB4D253c7a110241561B3eD6d632846dF7d4e9Af7
0
12
20480 [2.048e4]
```

The node holds the same values, which the recovery commands read:

```sh
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:6791/rpc -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"cartesi_getApplication","params":{"application":"ewapp"},"id":1}' \
  | jq '.result.data.withdrawal_config'
```

```json
{
  "guardian": "0x70997970c51812dc3a010c7d01b50e0d17dc79c8",
  "log2_leaves_per_account": "0x0",
  "log2_max_num_of_accounts": "0xc",
  "accounts_drive_start_index": "0x5000",
  "withdrawal_output_builder": "0xb4d253c7a110241561b3ed6d632846df7d4e9af7"
}
```

## Deposit

The devnet's `TestUsdc` starts with no supply, and anyone can mint it. Mint some to two devnet accounts, account 8 (the default sender of `cartesi deposit`) and account 7. The devnet accounts are unlocked, so `cast` can send from them without a key:

```sh
USDC=0x7a051EDffC0884cd88d4a377F4C87BE074CF6c81
ALICE=0x23618e81E3f5cdF7f54C3d65f7FBc0aBf5B21E8f
BOB=0x14dC79964da2C08b23698B3D3cc7Ca32193d9955
cast send $USDC 'mint(address,uint256)' $ALICE 1000000000 --unlocked --from $ALICE --rpc-url $RPC | grep '^status'
cast send $USDC 'mint(address,uint256)' $BOB 1000000000 --unlocked --from $BOB --rpc-url $RPC | grep '^status'
```

```text
status               1 (success)
status               1 (success)
```

`TestUsdc` has 6 decimals, so each account now holds 1000 USDC. Deposit 100 USDC from Alice and 250 USDC from Bob through the ERC-20 portal:

```sh
cartesi deposit erc20 --token $USDC 100
```

```text
- Approving 100 USDC...
✔ Approved 100 USDC
- Depositing 100 USDC to 0x19607994febf8381df4be89cd82cdd984285c7c0...
✔ Deposited 100 USDC to 0x19607994febf8381df4be89cd82cdd984285c7c0
```

```sh
cartesi deposit --from $BOB erc20 --token $USDC 250
```

```text
- Approving 250 USDC...
✔ Approved 250 USDC
- Depositing 250 USDC to 0x19607994febf8381df4be89cd82cdd984285c7c0...
✔ Deposited 250 USDC to 0x19607994febf8381df4be89cd82cdd984285c7c0
```

Emergency withdrawal pays out the balances of the last **accepted** epoch, so wait until the epoch holding both deposits is `CLAIM_ACCEPTED` (about a minute and a half with the flags above). Repeat this until it is:

```sh
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:6791/rpc -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"cartesi_listEpochs","params":{"application":"ewapp"},"id":1}' \
  | jq -c '.result.data[] | {index, status}'
```

```text
{"index":"0x4","status":"CLAIM_ACCEPTED"}
```

Now make two more deposits, 40 USDC from Bob and 15 USDC from Alice. You will foreclose before their epoch is accepted, so they stay unfinalized:

```sh
cartesi deposit --from $BOB erc20 --token $USDC 40
```

```text

✔ Approved 40 USDC
- Depositing 40 USDC to 0x19607994febf8381df4be89cd82cdd984285c7c0...
✔ Deposited 40 USDC to 0x19607994febf8381df4be89cd82cdd984285c7c0
```
